Motorcycle Touring the UK on £500

Think you need deep pockets to tour Britain by motorcycle? Think again. With smart planning, a tent, and a willingness to embrace simplicity, you can have a week of incredible riding for under £500. Here's the blueprint.

Budget Breakdown for 7 Days

  • Fuel: £150-180 (approximately 1,000 miles at current prices)
  • Camping: £70-100 (mix of paid campsites at £10-15/night and wild camping)
  • Food: £100-140 (self-catering with occasional pub lunches)
  • Attractions: £30-50 (most UK scenery is free — budget for one or two paid entries)
  • Emergency fund: £50-80 (always keep a buffer)
  • Total: £400-500

Fuel Economy Tips

Fuel is your biggest single expense. Reduce it intelligently:

  • Ride at a steady 55-60mph on A-roads instead of 70+. The fuel saving is dramatic, particularly on sportier bikes.
  • Use supermarket fuel stations (Tesco, Asda, Morrisons, Sainsbury's) — consistently 5-10p per litre cheaper than branded stations.
  • Keep your tyre pressures correct for loaded riding. Under-inflated tyres waste fuel.
  • Avoid unnecessary idling. Turn off at viewpoints and photo stops.

Accommodation on the Cheap

Accommodation is where budget touring really wins or loses. Your options:

  • Wild camping (Scotland): Completely free and legal under the Scottish Outdoor Access Code. Camp away from roads and buildings, leave no trace, and you have the best accommodation in Britain for free.
  • Basic campsites: £8-15 per night. A field, a tap, a toilet. That's often all you need.
  • Bothies (Scotland): Free mountain shelters maintained by the Mountain Bothies Association. Basic but atmospheric and free.
  • Community campsites: Some villages offer camping for a donation. Ask locally.

Eating on a Budget

Eating out at every meal will destroy a budget tour. Here's the strategy:

  • Breakfast: Cook at your campsite. Porridge and coffee cost pennies per serving.
  • Lunch: Supermarket meal deals (£3-4) or packed sandwiches from breakfast supplies.
  • Dinner: Cook simple one-pot meals at camp. Pasta, rice, and canned goods are cheap, calorie-dense, and easy to prepare. Treat yourself to a pub meal once or twice in the week.
  • Carry a refillable water bottle. Buying bottled water is an unnecessary expense in a country with excellent tap water.
Budget touring isn't about deprivation — it's about priorities. Spend money on fuel to reach the best roads and views. Save money on the things that matter less. A sunset over a Scottish loch costs nothing whether you're in a tent or a hotel.

Free Things to Do on Tour

Britain is incredibly generous with free experiences:

  • All national parks are free to enter and ride through
  • Most castles, ruins, and historical sites are visible (and photographable) from the road for free
  • Beaches, lochs, rivers, and waterfalls — all free
  • Mountain viewpoints and passes — free
  • National museums in Scotland are free (National Museum of Scotland, National Gallery, etc.)
  • Many English Heritage and Cadw sites are free to walk around externally

Money-Saving Route Tips

Avoid toll roads (the UK has very few, but the M6 Toll and some bridges charge). Take the free alternatives — they're often more scenic anyway. Plan routes that pass through towns with supermarkets for affordable resupplying. And the single best money-saving tip: head to Scotland, where wild camping and free attractions make budget touring easiest.

Where NOT to Cut Costs

Some things shouldn't be cheapened on tour:

  • Insurance — don't ride uninsured or underinsured to save money
  • Breakdown cover — the cost of one recovery without it exceeds your entire annual membership
  • Tyre condition — bald tyres aren't a budgeting choice, they're a safety hazard
  • Fuel — never risk running dry to save a few miles

With this approach, £500 buys you seven days of freedom, open roads, and some of the best scenery in Europe. Not bad at all.

Spring Gear Recommendations

Spring demands versatile gear. A textile touring jacket with removable thermal and waterproof liners handles the full range of March-May conditions. Pair it with layering base layers and you're equipped for frost and sunshine in the same day.

Gloves are especially important in spring — cold hands on a March morning transition to warm hands by April afternoon. Carry both winter and summer gloves until you're confident the cold has passed. A neck tube provides warmth on chilly mornings and stows in a pocket when the day warms up.

Wet Weather Alternatives

Even on your carefully planned dry route, rain will sometimes arrive. When it does, adjust your riding rather than abandoning the day. Slow down, increase following distances, and find indoor stops to wait out the worst showers. UK rain often comes in bands — a 30-minute wait at a cafe can see you emerge into sunshine.

The beauty of planning dry-side routes is that they're statistically more likely to be dry, not guaranteed. Over a week's touring, a dry-route strategy might give you 5-6 dry days instead of 3-4. That's a significant improvement in your touring experience and well worth the planning effort.

Microclimate Awareness

The UK has fascinating microclimates that riders can exploit. The Moray Firth coast around Nairn and Findhorn in Scotland is sometimes called the Scottish Riviera — it enjoys significantly drier, sunnier weather than the west coast. The rain shadow of the Pennines keeps northeast England drier than the northwest. And the Isles of Scilly off Cornwall enjoy the mildest, most Mediterranean-like climate in Britain.

Urban heat islands also affect riding conditions. Cities are typically 2-3 degrees warmer than surrounding countryside, which means less frost risk and earlier road drying after rain. A touring route that passes through major towns benefits from these temperature buffers on cold days. Conversely, climbing to altitude from a town means encountering conditions several degrees colder than the valley floor.
keyTakeaways: A week of UK touring is achievable for £400-500 with camping and self-catering.
Fuel is the biggest expense at £150-180 for around 1,000 miles; ride at 55-60mph and use supermarket stations.
Wild camping in Scotland is free, basic campsites cost £8-15, and bothies are free.
Cook breakfast and dinner at camp and use supermarket meal deals for lunch to protect the budget.
Never cut costs on insurance, breakdown cover, tyres or fuel safety.

faq.q: Can I really tour the UK for £500 a week?
faq.a: Yes. With a tent, self-catering and smart planning, a week comes in around £400 to £500. The typical breakdown is £150 to £180 fuel for roughly 1,000 miles, £70 to £100 camping, £100 to £140 food, £30 to £50 attractions and a £50 to £80 emergency buffer. Head to Scotland, where free wild camping makes budget touring easiest.

faq.q: How do I cut fuel costs?
faq.a: Fuel is your biggest single expense, so ride at a steady 55 to 60mph on A-roads instead of 70-plus, which saves dramatically on sportier bikes. Use supermarket stations such as Tesco, Asda, Morrisons and Sainsbury's, which are consistently 5 to 10p per litre cheaper than branded ones, keep tyres correctly inflated, and avoid idling at viewpoints.

faq.q: What are the cheapest places to sleep?
faq.a: Wild camping in Scotland is completely free and legal under the Scottish Outdoor Access Code. Basic campsites cost £8 to £15 per night for a field, a tap and a toilet, and bothies maintained by the Mountain Bothies Association are free. Some villages also offer community camping for a donation, so ask locally.

faq.q: How do I eat cheaply on tour?
faq.a: Cook porridge and coffee at your campsite for breakfast, use supermarket meal deals at £3 to £4 or packed sandwiches for lunch, and cook simple one-pot pasta or rice meals for dinner. Treat yourself to a pub meal once or twice in the week. Carry a refillable water bottle, as bottled water is a needless expense in the UK.

faq.q: Where should I never cut costs?
faq.a: Do not skimp on insurance, breakdown cover, tyre condition or fuel safety. Riding uninsured or on bald tyres is not budgeting, it is a hazard, and the cost of one recovery without breakdown cover exceeds an entire year's membership. Never risk running dry to save a few miles either.
